procedural_history.originating_court: District Magistrate, Jammu; Government of the State of Jammu and Kashmir
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of detention dated 5th September, 1956, issued by the Government of the State of Jammu and Kashmir under sub-section (2) of section 3 of the Jammu and Kashmir Preventive Detention Act, 2011, confirming and continuing an earlier detention order passed by the District Magistrate, Jammu, on 1st May, 1956, under sub-section (2) of section 3 of the same Act.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: N/A (The case originated directly in the Supreme Court under Article 32 of the Constitution.)
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner filed an application in the Supreme Court under Article 32 of the Constitution seeking a writ of habeas corpus against the State of Jammu and Kashmir, challenging his detention.

directions: Directed the release forthwith of the detenue

issue.issue_text: Whether a preventive detention order is valid when it is based on multiple grounds, and some of those grounds are found to be non-existent or irrelevant.

facts: A preventive detention order was issued against an individual based on multiple grounds or reasons.
Upon review, some of the grounds cited in the order were found to be non-existent, irrelevant, or unsubstantiated.
law: The validity of a preventive detention order depends entirely on the "subjective satisfaction" of the detaining authority.
This subjective satisfaction must be properly based on all the reasons on which the order purports to be based.
Preventive detention is a serious invasion of personal liberty, and constitutional safeguards against its improper use must be strictly enforced.
application: The Court reasoned that if some of the grounds for detention are invalid, it is impossible to determine how much each ground influenced the detaining authority's decision.
The Court cannot speculate whether the authority would have been satisfied and issued the order if it had only considered the valid grounds.

To uphold the detention order based on the remaining valid grounds would require the Court to substitute its own objective judgment for the subjective satisfaction of the executive authority, which is not permissible.

Therefore, if even one of the grounds is found to be non-existent or irrelevant, it vitiates the entire detention order because the foundation of the authority's subjective satisfaction is compromised.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a preventive detention order is invalid and must be quashed if it is based on multiple grounds and some of those grounds are found to be non-existent or irrelevant.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a preventive detention order is valid when it is based on multiple grounds, and some of those grounds are found to be non-existent or irrelevant.
appellant_arguments: The detention order is invalid because it was based on multiple grounds (smuggling shaffon cloth, zari, and mercury), but some of those grounds were non-existent or irrelevant, as shaffon cloth and zari were not essential goods.

The subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority was based on all the grounds collectively. If some grounds are invalid, it is impossible for a court to determine what the authority's decision would have been based only on the remaining valid grounds.

Preventive detention is a serious invasion of personal liberty, and constitutional safeguards must be strictly enforced. If any of the stated grounds for detention are flawed, the entire order must be considered invalid.
respondent_arguments: The detention order should be considered valid as long as at least one of the grounds is legitimate and sufficient to justify the detention.
The smuggling of mercury was a valid ground for detention, and the order can be sustained on this ground alone, even if the other grounds concerning shaffon cloth and zari are found to be irrelevant.

statutes.act_name: Jammu and Kashmir Preventive Detention Act, 2011

cases.principle: If a detention order is based on multiple grounds, and one of those grounds is found to be irrelevant or illusory, the entire detention order is vitiated. A court cannot assess the extent to which each ground influenced the detaining authority's subjective satisfaction, and to uphold the order on the remaining grounds would be to substitute an objective judicial test for the subjective decision of the executive.

Where a detention order is based on multiple grounds taken together, and some are found to be non-existent or irrelevant, the entire exercise of power is bad because the subjective satisfaction of the authority is vitiated.

cases.case_name: Dr. Ram Krishan Bhardwaj v. The State of Delhi
cases.principle: Preventive detention is a serious invasion of personal liberty, and constitutional safeguards must be strictly enforced. The constitutional requirement to provide grounds for detention must be satisfied with respect to each of the grounds communicated to the detenu. If this is not done for any single ground, the detention is not in accordance with the 'procedure established by law' under Article 21.

cases.case_name: Shibban Lal Saksena v. The State of U.P.
cases.principle: The power to issue a detention order depends entirely on the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority. If one of the grounds for detention is later found to be non-existent, the detention order cannot be upheld on the remaining grounds, as it is impossible to determine how the invalid ground influenced the authority's satisfaction.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: If a detention order is based on the subjective satisfaction of an authority derived from multiple grounds, and some of those grounds are subsequently found to be non-existent or irrelevant, the entire detention order is invalid. A court cannot sever the invalid grounds to uphold the order on the remaining ones, as it is impossible to determine to what extent the invalid grounds influenced the authority's subjective decision.
obiter: The court must be satisfied that the vague or irrelevant grounds are significant enough that, if excluded, they might reasonably have affected the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority.
Preventive detention is a serious invasion of personal liberty, and constitutional safeguards against its improper exercise must be jealously watched and enforced by the Court.
A court is not competent to inquire into the truth or otherwise of the facts mentioned as grounds for detention.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Where a preventive detention order is based on the subjective satisfaction of an authority with reference to multiple grounds taken together, the order is invalid if some of those grounds are found to be non-existent or irrelevant. This is because it is impossible for a court to determine what the subjective satisfaction of the authority would have been if the invalid grounds were excluded. To uphold the order on the remaining valid grounds would be to improperly substitute the objective judgment of the court for the subjective satisfaction of the executive authority.
legal_tests_applied: The Subjective Satisfaction Test: The validity of a detention order depends entirely on the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority, and a court cannot substitute its own objective test to determine if the remaining valid grounds are sufficient to sustain the order.

The Non-Severability Test: When multiple grounds form a collective basis for the detaining authority's satisfaction, the invalidity of some grounds vitiates the entire order, as the court cannot sever the bad reasons from the good ones to see what the authority would have decided.

The Materiality Test: For an order to be invalidated, the court must be satisfied that the vague or irrelevant grounds are significant enough that their exclusion might reasonably have affected the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority; grounds of a 'comparatively unessential nature' might not be sufficient to invalidate the order.
policy_considerations: Preventive detention is a serious invasion of personal liberty, and the meagre constitutional safeguards against its improper exercise must be jealously watched and enforced by the Court.

Upholding a detention order when some grounds are invalid would be to substitute an objective judicial test for the subjective decision of the executive authority, which is against the legislative policy underlying the statute.
